prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: FAA NextGen aims to raise National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency; adverse en route weather causes ~70% of US delays. System of interest: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3), integrated ground/aircraft decision aids seeking efficient weather-avoidance routes, responding to weather and Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), sustaining en route/arrival metering. Subset: NASA Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), cruise phase, using existing weather/airspace/traffic data and ATM automation. Current system: FAA traffic managers set static Flow Constrained Areas (FCA) and Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP, aka Playbook routes) 2-8 h ahead. Airline flight dispatchers file flight plans >=45 min before push-back. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) is strategic only. Controllers, dispatchers and flight crews request amendments manually; crews use flight management systems and limited-range on-board weather radar. Gap: no automation flags expired constraints or savings. DWR: ground-based trajectory automation that continuously, automatically analyzes in-flight aircraft in en route airspace at/above 10,000 ft, updating trajectories as new radar track and flight plan data arrive. It seeks simple time/fuel-saving route corrections (like today's operations) to weather avoidance routes or wind-favorable direct-to routes, accounting for convective weather, traffic conflicts, sector congestion, special use airspace, FAA restrictions. Logic: compute reference direct route from Maneuver Start Point (MSP; programmable, default 5 min downstream of present position or first point in high altitude airspace) to default Return Capture Fix (RCF; downstream waypoint on current flight plan approximating an operationally acceptable direct clearance given airspace and destination arrival limits). If wind-corrected savings >= user-defined minimum (default 5 min), flight assumed on weather avoidance route; route probed for weather/traffic conflicts; on weather conflict DWR inserts 1-2 auxiliary waypoints for minimum-delay route; MSP/waypoints optionally adjusted for integrated weather+traffic resolution. If solution still meets threshold, DWR posts route advisory to alert list on user display. User (controller/dispatcher/crew) may view/modify before requesting/issuing clearance; UI must strongly warn if modified trial trajectory conflicts with forecast weather/traffic. DWR extends NASA Direct-To tool (1998-2001); Direct-To routes meeting threshold appear as advisories even without weather. Constraints modeled as polygons. No explicit

Document units:
U0064: Figure 1: DWR Concept Overview Inserted auxiliary waypoints are initially computed using fix-radial-distance points which may be placed anywhere for a minimum delay solution.
U0065: A snap-to named fix option automatically replaces any auxiliary waypoints with nearby named fixes for ease of use in voice-based operations.
U0066: Snap-To solutions that avoid weather, or optionally weather and traffic, are posted to the DWR alert list if they meet the minimum flight-time savings criteria.
U0067: The current flight plan trajectory and the DWR-advised trajectory are both analyzed for conflict with congested airspace sectors and with Special Use Airspace (SUA).
U0068: The traffic congestion and SUA status are incorporated into the user interface display so the user may consider these factors when evaluating the DWR route advisory.
U0069: By clicking the DWR advisory the user activates an automated interactive trial planning function to visualize the route and if necessary modify the RCF, the MSP, and any inserted auxiliary waypoints.
U0070: Flight-time savings and weather and traffic conflicts status update rapidly (within 1 sec) and automatically as the user modifies the DWR route.
U0071: Figure 2: DWR Automation Process The RCF is a downstream fix on the current Center route of flight at which the DWR route correction rejoins the original flight plan trajectory.
U0072: A limit function unique to the particular airspace region (i.e., unique to each Center’s airspace) determines the default RCF to be used for DWR route correction computations.
U0073: The purpose of the limit function is to define a default RCF for any flight given its present position and current route of flight such that a direct route from present aircraft track position to the RCF is generally operationally acceptable if weather were not a factor.
U0074: The RCF is a function of Center airspace and arrival routing limits, and may be a function of other factors such as the particular routing (city pair routing for example) in the given Center airspace and the first-tier adjacent Center airspace.
U0075: The RCF is generally not the last fix within the Center boundary where the aircraft is currently located.
U0076: The NASA DWR automation for Fort Worth Center employs a limit rectangle that extends roughly 200 nmi beyond the ZFW boundary (see Figure 3).
